analysis.one_liner: Gives unauthorized immigrants a long path to legal status, paid for with a border surge and mandatory work checks.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it 68-32 in June 2013, but the House never held a vote, and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let unauthorized immigrants who have been in the country since before the end of 2011 apply for temporary legal status, with a possible green card years later after background checks, fees, and employment requirements. The price: no green cards until the government builds 700 miles of border fencing, nearly doubles the Border Patrol to 38,405 agents, and puts a mandatory E-Verify employment check in place for every hire in America. It also expands skilled-worker and guest-worker visa programs and hands $1.5 billion to summer and year-round jobs for low-income young people.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly 11 million undocumented residents could come out of the shadows: work and travel authorization, protection from removal, and, after meeting border-security triggers and waiting periods, lawful permanent residence and eventual citizenship. Young people brought here as children get a faster track under the DREAM Act title. Farmworkers get an earned 'blue card' path to residency. Asylum seekers no longer face a one-year filing deadline, and unaccompanied children in deportation court would get appointed lawyers. Micronesian citizens living lawfully in the U.S. become Medicaid-eligible, low-income 16-to-25-year-olds get a $1.5 billion jobs fund, and skilled immigrant workers get larger visa quotas plus whistleblower protections against abusive H-1B employers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Undocumented residents, farmworkers, DREAMers, low-income youth

how_it_helps.text: Grants registered provisional immigrant (RPI) status to unauthorized immigrants present since December 31, 2011 who pass background checks, pay fees and penalties, and clear tax liabilities — letting them work and travel legally and barring their removal.
Sets a route from RPI status to a green card through the bill's merit-based system, and to citizenship, though not until the border-security certification triggers are met.
Creates a DREAM Act track letting those who entered before age 16 and finished high school, college, or military service adjust to permanent residence on a faster timeline.
Gives agricultural workers 'blue card' status and an earned path to permanent residency after continued farm employment, plus correction of their Social Security records.
Eliminates the one-year deadline for filing asylum claims and requires appointed counsel in removal cases involving unaccompanied children and people with serious mental disabilities.
Appropriates $1.5 billion for a Youth Jobs Fund providing summer and year-round jobs for low-income 16-to-25-year-olds, funded by a visa surcharge on employers.

Raises the H-1B cap to 115,000 with a mechanism reaching 180,000, adds 25,000 STEM slots, and funds low-income STEM scholarships from employer fees — while capping firms whose workforce is majority H-1B/L visa holders and strengthening whistleblower and Department of Labor complaint protections.
Makes citizens of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, and Palau lawfully residing in the U.S. eligible for Medicaid, and extends housing assistance to battered immigrants.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers front $46.3 billion for the border build-out (with $8.3 billion of fee collections later routed back for deficit reduction and ongoing costs charged to applicants through fees and surcharges). Every U.S. employer must eventually enroll in the mandatory E-Verify system for all new hires, a civil violation for those who don't. Applicants pay processing fees, fines, and a $400 fine for blue-card adjustment. Lawful workers face a new employment-verification database affecting every job application, and U.S. workers in tech and low-wage trades face enlarged visa competition. Immigrants themselves give up access to federal means-tested benefits for years and give up the diversity visa lottery and sibling visas.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, all employers, and visa applicants

drawbacks.text: Makes E-Verify mandatory for every employer within roughly four to five years, with fraud-resistant Social Security cards as the backbone — a de facto national employment screening system where database errors could wrongly block lawful workers from jobs.

Conditions green cards on triggers the government may take years to meet: 700 miles of pedestrian fencing, 38,405 Border Patrol agents, full E-Verify, and exit systems — while letting the Secretary waive nearly any law to build border infrastructure, with lawsuits limited to constitutional claims in federal district court.

Creates large new guest-worker programs — W-1 visas scaling up to 200,000 and an H-2B returning-worker exemption — in which workers lose status if unemployed for 60 days, cannot bring spouses, and are excluded from federal need-based benefits.
Keeps RPI and blue-card holders ineligible for federal means-tested benefits and bars federal agencies from waiving those restrictions for years, while charging applicants fees, penalties, and fines.

Repeals the diversity visa lottery as of October 2014 and eliminates the visa category for brothers and sisters of U.S. citizens, trading family reunification for a points-based system weighted toward education and employment.
Spends tens of billions on border fencing, sensors, and aircraft — a list of specific towers, cameras, and drones for each border sector — money many economists consider of doubtful effectiveness.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The legalization headline is real and enormous: a vulnerable population of millions would gain lawful work, protection from deportation, and eventually citizenship — the largest such benefit since 1986. But the bill bought those votes with an expensive border build-out, a universal employment-verification database that could misfire on lawful workers, and expanded guest-worker programs that create a sub-tier of workers without full rights. The triggers also mean the green-card promise depends on certification politics years later. It was a genuine trade, designed to satisfy both sides, not a clean win for anyone.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it 68-32 on June 27, 2013 after three weeks of floor votes, but the House never brought it up for a vote, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Introduced April 16, 2013 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which held hearings in April and a markup in May before reporting the bill with a substitute amendment on May 28 and placing it on the Senate calendar.
The Senate moved to the bill in June 2013, first clearing a procedural vote to proceed 82-15 and then the motion itself 84-15.

During floor consideration the Senate waived budget-law objections 68-30, invoked cloture on the substitute amendment 67-31, agreed to the committee substitute 68-32, and passed the bill 68-32 on June 27, 2013.
The House Judiciary Committee held a hearing in May 2013, but the House never scheduled a vote on the Senate-passed bill, and it died at the end of the 113th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: House leaders who never scheduled a vote are better off, along with opponents on both flanks who preferred the status quo — and employers who depend on unauthorized labor avoided the new verification system. The roughly 11 million undocumented residents remained without legal status.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: House leaders who blocked the vote

for.name: Sen. Charles E. Schumer
for.role: Lead sponsor (D-NY), Gang of Eight author
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its drafting and Senate passage.

for.name: Sen. Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the Senate floor, scheduled three weeks of consideration, and managed cloture votes through final passage.

for.name: 52 of 52 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on every key roll call, including final passage 68-32.

for.name: 14 of 46 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, supplying the margin that let the bill clear the Senate.

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Publicly pressed Congress to pass comprehensive immigration reform.

against.name: Speaker John Boehner
against.what_they_did: Declined to bring the Senate-passed bill to the House floor for a vote, so the House never acted on it.

against.name: 32 of 46 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on cloture and final passage.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee majority
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing in May 2013 but never marked up or reported an immigration bill of its own.

sides.party_line_note: In the Senate the bill was overwhelmingly Democratic — all 52 Democrats and both independents voted yes, while Republicans split 14-32 on final passage — and the House, where Republicans held the majority, never voted at all.

industries.industry: Border security contractors and surveillance-technology vendors
industries.note: The bill appropriates $46.3 billion: $30 billion for 19,200 more Border Patrol agents, over $7.5 billion for 700 miles of fencing, and detailed minimum lists of towers, cameras, sensors, and drones for each border sector. This money flows to DHS procurement regardless of whether it measurably improves security.

Farm employers gain a legalized existing workforce through blue cards and a new W-3/W-4 guest-worker program replacing H-2A, with written contracts and wage terms. But the program bars spouses and derivatives, excludes workers from federal benefits, and requires departures between stays.

The H-1B cap rises to 115,000 with an escalator to 180,000, plus 25,000 STEM slots and new entrepreneur visas. In exchange, firms face per-petition fees of $1,000-$2,500, a cap on companies whose U.S. workforce is majority H-1B/L holders, and stronger whistleblower and Labor Department complaint tools.

industries.industry: Hospitality, construction, and other low-wage labor-intensive employers
industries.note: A new W-1 guest-worker visa scales from 20,000 to as many as 200,000 positions annually, and returning H-2B workers are exempted from caps. Guardrails exist — recruitment of U.S. workers first and a bar on W hiring where construction unemployment tops 8.5% — but the programs add labor competition in low-wage trades.

industries.industry: EB-5 real estate developers and regional centers
industries.note: The temporary EB-5 investor-visa regional center program becomes permanent, with petition preapproval and premium processing, locking in a channel that converts foreign investment (and foreign investors' wealth) into U.S. residency.

Within roughly four to five years every employer must use the mandatory E-Verify system for all new hires, with civil penalties for nonparticipation — a compliance cost for all, though it also levels the field against competitors who rely on unauthorized labor.
